analysis.one_liner: Removes the income cap on Social Security payroll taxes and boosts seniors' cost-of-living increases.
analysis.headline: A bill to lift the cap on wages taxed for Social Security, with 10 Democratic cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would remove the ceiling (about $118,500 in 2015) on the wages that are taxed to fund Social Security, so that high earners and their employers pay the payroll tax on every dollar of wages, not just the first $118,500. The new revenue would go into the Social Security trust funds, extending the program's solvency. It would also replace the standard inflation index with a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers when calculating Social Security and Medicare adjustments, because seniors' spending is weighted more toward health care.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, disabled workers, and survivors who draw Social Security, in two ways: the trust funds would be replenished by tax revenue from wages above the cap, and annual benefit increases would be calculated on an index built around seniors' actual spending, which typically rises faster than the general index. Medicare's limits and payment updates would also rise with an elderly-focused index. Future beneficiaries gain from a more solvent program.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the cap on wages subject to the Social Security payroll tax, so income above $118,500 (in 2015 dollars) would be taxed like all other wages [S2][S3].
It steers the new payroll tax revenue into the Social Security trust funds, improving the program's long-term solvency [S2][S3].

It directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers and use it to set Social Security and Medicare adjustments, reflecting spending patterns typical of people 62 and older [S2][S3].
The changes take effect starting January 1, 2016, for wages and taxable years after December 31, 2015 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and their employers pay the most: an employee earning well above the cap would owe the 6.2% employee payroll tax on wages above it, employers would owe the matching 6.2%, and self-employed people would owe the combined rate on income above the cap. Medicare providers and plans also face higher payment updates because their formulas would switch to the elderly-focused index, which grows faster because it weights medical costs heavily — a cost that flows to the federal budget and, ultimately, taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, their employers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes directly on high-income households and on businesses with high-paid employees, including the employer matching share, starting in 2016 [S3].

Because the Social Security benefit formula does not increase benefits for income above the current cap, high earners would pay the tax on that income without receiving proportionally higher benefits — a deliberate transfer, but one that critics argue weakens the traditional link between what workers contribute and what they receive [S2][S3].
Switching Medicare payment updates to the elderly-focused index would raise federal Medicare spending, since that index grows faster because of its heavy weighting of medical costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most working people and retirees the benefits are large: a more secure Social Security program and annual increases that better track senior living costs. The costs fall narrowly on high earners and their employers, plus somewhat higher Medicare spending that affects the federal budget broadly. The main design criticism is not the size of the transfer but that it is explicit — the wealthiest workers pay into the system without a matching increase in their own benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees in April 2015, was referred to a subcommittee that November, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the FAIR Social Security Act on April 23, 2015, with five original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
On November 16, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — the last action the bill ever received [S5].
Ten Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from the House [S4].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the bill's action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners whose wages above the cap remain untaxed for Social Security, the employers who would have paid the matching tax on those wages, and anyone preferring the payroll tax base stay as it is. Social Security beneficiaries did not get the solvency fix or the higher benefit index.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners whose wages stayed untaxed

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Social Security payroll tax cap and apply an elderly-focused cost-of-living index.

for.name: 10 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee record shows no action after the referral [S5].

against.role: Chair of the secondary committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions on November 16, 2015, where it sat without further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was never brought to a vote, so no roll-call exists; every sponsor and cosponsor on record was a Democrat, and the committees that buried it were chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: They would pay the 6.2% employee payroll tax (12.4% for the self-employed) on all wages above the roughly $118,500 cap, without a proportional increase in their own benefits. That cost is what funds the solvency gain for beneficiaries [S2][S3].
Employers owe a matching 6.2% payroll tax on wages above the cap once it is repealed, raising labor costs for firms concentrated at the top of the pay scale [S3].

Hospital, physician, and plan payment updates would switch to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, whose medical-cost weighting makes it rise faster than the general index, producing larger Medicare payment increases financed by the federal budget [S3].
